items.title: Emile Barnes Interview, 1962-01-03
items.q: Well I did. I did got it from Big R. Louis

ctx.x: It's a special chorus. I know George Lewis plays it, Piku played it, Burbank played it. I believe Big R. Louis. Well you told me once, Mealy, or am I wrong, that you heard it from Big R. Louis.

Well I did. I did got it from Big R. Louis, and if I'm mistaken, I think Big R. Louis, he come up with it. If I'm mistaken, I'm because I really caught in my mind now, it's a lemon. I don't know, they don't play the outside of him. You take, for instance, George Braquet. You take, how do you call them that, Piku, none of them didn't make it. Oh, they didn't play it then?

items.title: Emile Barnes Interview, 1960-07-29
items.q: Now your man, your good band man, real band man, that was Louis, which we called Big Eye Louis.

ctx.x: How about Bacay? What were some of the things you liked about the way Bacay played? Peter Bacay? No, George Bacay. What? Bacay. Bacay. Oh, George? Yeah.

Well, I'll tell you how George was. He was a, to me he was a sweet clarinet player. You know, he just took his time and made that. You know, he didn't rough it out. But he had that one way. Now for a band man, he wasn't that much, he ain't a band man. But he was a tough man in the parade. And you could hear him way down there but so sweet. Now your man, your good band man, real band man, that was Louis, which we called Big Eye Louis. In the orchestra you mean? Yeah. In the orchestra. That's really, Charlie can…

You know that time you cut the records with Charlie Love? Do you remember that? Was it on St. Louis Street near Decatur? That's right, yeah. Uh huh. Well it seemed to me as the evening went on, you changed your whole tone and style and everything, you know? Yeah. You played different. You played different that night from any other time I heard you. I don't think they issued the stuff, you know, late in the evening where you began to play very different.
